domain: Transportation Engineering / Institutional Coordination / Historical Path Dependency
topic_summary: Analysis of the traffic convention mandating which side of the road vehicles drive on (right-hand vs left-hand). This is a coordination standard with no inherent physical superiority of either choice, but with massive switching costs once established.

key_entities: National traffic authorities (enforcement bodies setting and maintaining the standard)
Vehicle manufacturers (design infrastructure around dominant convention)
International border crossings (sites where conventions collide)
key_tensions: Coordination efficiency vs switching cost inertia (standardization gains vs transition impossibility)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The shared commitment that all vehicles within a jurisdiction must use the same side of the road
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: State traffic law enforcement; legitimacy grounded in coordination necessity rather than interpretive tradition
commitment_system_recognition.kernel_collapse_reason: All supposed 'readings' of this topic converge on the same constraint structure: a coordination standard with arbitrary choice but mandatory uniformity. Right-hand and left-hand are not different interpretive commitments producing different constraints — they are two instances of the identical constraint type (coordination rope) with flipped parameters. No party 'reads' the coordination requirement differently; they merely instantiated different arbitrary choices historically. The disagreement is about WHICH standard to adopt, not about what KIND of constraint the standard creates.

axes.human_readable: Coordination Lock-In (Network Effects of Handedness Choice)
axes.structural_delta: Once a handedness convention is established, switching costs (vehicle redesign, infrastructure, retraining, accident risk during transition) create irreversible lock-in
axes.primary_observable: Cost estimate for full national handedness switch; number of countries that have successfully switched post-1950
axes.selection_reason: Core structural constraint; upstream to all other dynamics

axes.structural_delta: At borders between right-hand and left-hand jurisdictions, infrastructure must manage the transition (lane crossovers, signage, accident risk)
axes.primary_observable: Accident rates at handedness-transition borders vs same-handedness borders; infrastructure cost per transition point
axes.selection_reason: Structurally distinct observable (border infrastructure vs national switching cost); downstream consequence of lock-in

axes.structural_delta: Vehicle manufacturers design for dominant global convention (right-hand traffic = left-hand drive vehicles), creating cost asymmetry for minority-convention markets
axes.primary_observable: Price differential for right-hand-drive vehicles in right-hand-traffic markets; production volume ratios
axes.selection_reason: Deferred: captured indirectly via coordination_lock_in rope; manufacturing asymmetry is a downstream consequence of the same network effect observable

deferred_axes.structural_delta: Vehicle design asymmetry favoring dominant global convention
deferred_axes.deferral_reason: Downstream consequence of coordination_lock_in with overlapping observable (both measure network effect costs); limited independent structural yield

omegas.description: Topic was flagged as contested kernel but analysis reveals no genuine readings. Right-hand vs left-hand are not different interpretive commitments — they are two instances of the same coordination constraint with arbitrary parameter choice. The 'contest' is historical (which choice was made) not structural (what kind of constraint exists).

Does pedestrian flow convention (which side of sidewalk/stairway) correlate with vehicle handedness? If so, is it a separate rope or the same coordination constraint extended to non-vehicular traffic?

Is there any measurable safety difference between right-hand and left-hand traffic for populations with different handedness distributions? If yes, the rope may have a weak mountain component (neurological asymmetry).
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 1 (Operational Medium) — model assumes pure coordination, but human cognitive asymmetry may introduce physical constraint

omegas.description: For countries that inherited handedness from colonial powers, is the lock-in a rope (coordination) or a piton (atrophied sovereignty)? Post-independence switching attempts (e.g., Samoa 2009) suggest some view it as reversible.

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Topic is structurally simpler than kernel flag suggested — pure coordination problem with no contested interpretive layer.
